Client intake questionnaire for freelancers: 15 questions grouped by goals, deliverables, constraints and who decides

2026-11-21

If you freelance, this may sound familiar: the discovery call went well, the client sounded clear, and you wrote a quote. Then week two arrives and it turns out "a few pages" meant twelve, the text "is nearly ready" (it isn't), and a business partner you've never heard of wants to see the designs.

None of that was hidden on purpose. Nobody asked. A short client intake questionnaire, sent after the first conversation and before you quote, is a cheap way to ask.

This article gives you a complete questionnaire to copy, grouped into four parts: goals, deliverables, constraints and who decides. It also covers the covering email, what to do with vague answers, and how each answer becomes a line in your scope summary.

Not legal advice. The questionnaire collects information so you can describe and price the work. It isn't a contract, and the client's answers don't form one. Payment terms, ownership, liability and cancellation belong in a contract, ideally one reviewed by a qualified lawyer where you work.

Why four groups

You could ask thirty questions. Clients tend to answer long forms quickly and thinly, though, and you'll still end up asking follow-ups. Grouping does two jobs:

  1. The client sees why you're asking. "Who gives the final yes?" can feel nosy on its own. Under a heading called Who decides, it reads as normal project planning.
  2. You can see what's missing. Each group feeds a specific part of your quote. If one group comes back blank, you know which part of the quote is a guess.
Group What it tells you Where it goes in the scope summary
Goals What "worked" means to the client The goal line, and how you'll judge requests later
Deliverables What they expect to receive, and what they supply Deliverables, client responsibilities, "not included"
Constraints Time, money, tools and history Timeline, assumptions, price
Who decides Who gives feedback and who approves The feedback and approval line

The questionnaire (copy and paste)

Delete the questions that don't fit the project. A shorter form that comes back complete is more useful than a long one that comes back half-filled.

PROJECT QUESTIONNAIRE: [PROJECT NAME]

A line or two per question is plenty. If you don't know an
answer yet, say so: that's something we can work out together.
No passwords or logins here, please.

GOALS
1. In a sentence or two, what is this project for?
2. Once it's finished, what will be different? How would you
   notice?
3. Who is it mainly for (customers, staff, partners, investors)?
4. Why now? Is there an event, season or launch it needs to be
   ready for?

DELIVERABLES
5. What do you expect to receive, and how many of each? (For
   example: 6 pages, 4 articles, 2 logo versions.) A rough
   count is fine.
6. For each item, what does "finished" look like? (For example:
   live on your website, a print-ready file, a draft your team
   will edit.)
7. Which parts will you or your team provide (text, photos,
   product details, data, access to accounts)? When could they
   be ready?
8. Is there anything you'd like eventually, but not as part of
   this project?

CONSTRAINTS
9. When do you need it? Is that date fixed or flexible, and
   what's behind it?
10. What budget range do you have in mind? A range is fine.
11. Are there tools, platforms or brand rules we must use or
    avoid?
12. Has a similar project gone wrong before? What happened?

WHO DECIDES
13. Who will send feedback on drafts?
14. Who gives the final yes? Will anyone else see the work before
    it's finished (a partner, manager, board, legal or compliance
    check)?
15. When drafts arrive, how quickly can you usually reply?

Please return this by [DATE]. Within [NUMBER] working days
I'll send any follow-up questions, and after that a short
written scope summary for you to review.

The covering email

Subject: [Project name]: a few questions before I quote

Hi [NAME],

Thanks for the call. Before I put a price together, I'd like to check I've understood the project properly. The questions below should take about 15 minutes, and short answers are fine.

If anything doesn't apply, skip it. If you'd rather talk it through, reply and we'll book 20 minutes instead.

Could you send it back by [DATE]?

[YOUR NAME]

The "talk it through" option matters. Some clients would rather speak than write. In that case, use the same questions as your call agenda and send your notes back for them to confirm. That way you still end up with the answers in writing.

Why each group earns its place

Goals (questions 1-4)

Question 2 is the one to watch. "A fresh look" isn't an outcome. "People can book a table without phoning" is. When you have an outcome, you can test later requests against it: does this new idea help with what we agreed the project is for?

Question 4 shows you whether the deadline is real. "Our trade show is on the 14th" is a fixed date. "We'd like it soon" isn't.

Deliverables (questions 5-8)

Question 5 sets the count. Question 6 sets the finish line, which is where many disagreements start: you think "done" means a file, and the client thinks it means a live page with the text in place.

Question 7 is your dependency list in the client's own words. Anything they supply becomes a client responsibility with a date. Question 8 does quiet work too. It brings "phase two" wishes to the surface now, so they go in your "not included" list instead of turning up as mid-project requests.

Constraints (questions 9-12)

Asking for a budget range feels awkward. Without it, though, you can't tell whether to propose the full version or a smaller first phase. Ask for a range, not a number, and accept "not sure yet".

Question 12 is optional, but the answers are often revealing. A client who says "the last designer disappeared for a month" is telling you that regular updates matter to them. One who says "the last one kept charging extra" is telling you to explain your change process early and clearly.

Who decides (questions 13-15)

This group helps prevent the late-stage surprise of a new opinion arriving at the final review. If the person who approves is not the person you've been talking to, you want to know before you quote, so you can plan for their review.

Question 15 gives you a realistic timeline. If the client usually needs a week to reply, a two-week project with three rounds of feedback isn't two weeks.

When the answers come back vague

Vague answers aren't a red flag on their own. Most clients haven't had to think about these things before. Treat a vague answer as a prompt for one follow-up question, not as a reason to guess.

Vague answer Follow-up question
Q2: "Just make it look more professional" "If a new customer saw the finished version, what would you want them to do next?"
Q5: "A few pages" / "some posts" "If you had to name them, which ones? A rough list is fine."
Q6: "Just get it done" "When you picture it finished, is it live, or a file you'll use yourselves?"
Q7: "We'll sort the content out" "Who on your side will write it, and roughly when could the first batch be ready?"
Q9: "ASAP" "Is there a date after which it's much less useful to you?"
Q10: left blank "Would it help if I suggested two options, a smaller first phase and the full version?"
Q14: "Just me" "Is there anyone who'd want to see it before it goes live, even briefly?"

If the whole brief is thin, the AI hidden-dependency check walks through one prompt that lists what's missing, with a worked example. Check its output yourself. It suggests questions to ask. It doesn't replace your judgement.

Turning answers into scope lines

The questionnaire only pays off if the answers end up in writing that the client confirms. Here's how each question maps to your scope summary:

  • Goal line: questions 1-2, in the client's words where possible.
  • Deliverables: question 5 for the count, question 6 for "done when". For example: "6 blog posts of about 1,000 words, delivered as Google Docs. Done when approved."
  • Client responsibilities: question 7, each item with a date.
  • Not included: question 8, written in a friendly way. "A members' area isn't part of this project. Happy to quote it as a next phase."
  • Timeline: questions 4, 9 and 15 together.
  • Assumptions: question 11, plus anything you inferred and want the client to confirm.
  • Feedback and approval: questions 13-14. Name one person who sends combined feedback and one person who approves.

For revision rounds and feedback windows, the guide to how many revisions to include has wording you can adapt. Once the project is running, the out-of-scope request email guide covers what to say when something new comes up.

Where the questionnaire sits in onboarding

  1. Discovery call or email exchange.
  2. Send the questionnaire.
  3. Chase vague answers with one follow-up each.
  4. Check for dependencies, then write the quote and the scope summary.
  5. Client confirms the summary in writing; contract and kickoff follow.

The client onboarding checklist shows every step from the first conversation to kickoff. It includes a shorter 12-question version of this brief if you'd like something lighter.

The limits

  • It doesn't replace the conversation. The questionnaire collects facts. Tone, trust and the questions you didn't think to ask still come from talking.
  • Answers change. If the client's answers change after you quote, treat that as a change to the project, not a correction.
  • It isn't a contract. It informs your scope summary and your contract. It doesn't stand in for either.
